To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

songbirds have developed a neural pathway that mediates the control of learned vocalizations, which is distinct from the pathways mediating control over innate vocalizations, such as calls and alarm cries.

the brain pathways mediating control over the muscles of the syrnx, the respiratory apparatus and the vocal tract are distinct, that the pathway for control over syringeal muscles originates in the telancephalon and projects to the syringeal motoneurons via the occipitomesecephalic tract, and that the pathways controlling the respiratory and vocal tract muscles originate from the medulla and project to premotor neurons of the brainstem.
the brainstem pathways mediate the coordination of the respiratory and syringeal motor systems during song production in songbirds.
In summary, our research is concerned with

elucidating the neural mechanisms underlying the control of learned vocal behavior, with particular emphasis upon the neural pathways and their interactions, and with the role of the telencephalic control system in this process.
elucidating the organization of the neural pathways controlling the vocal apparatus of birds.
the neural pathways that control song production in songbirds.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the neural pathways controlling the production of birdsong have a number of similarities and differences from those of mammals.

the neural pathways for the control and coordination of song production are remarkably similar to those for speech production in humans, but the pathways mediating control and coordination of vocalizations in other animals are different from those in songbirds.

birdsong production is controlled by a brainstem pathway that is similar to the vocal control system in other animals and that birdsong production also requires the involvement of the telencephalic system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the neural pathways mediating vocalization in songbirds are very similar to those in mammals.

the brainstem pathways mediate the production of species specific vocalizations and that the telencephalic pathways are involved with the production of learned, or learned-like vocalizations, such as song.
the neural control of song in songbirds is similar to the control of speech in humans.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the neural control of vocalization in songbirds is a good model system for studying the neural control of speech in humans.
songbirds provide a model system that is useful for understanding the neural control of vocal behavior in general.
the telencephalic pathways for the control song production in birds are similar to the telencephalically mediated vocal control pathways in humans.
